claim: Naming the shared relation (relational label) at encoding and/or retrieval raises cross-domain relational reminding in adults; unaided retrieval favours same-domain matches (4.58 vs 1.56 of 10). Labels at both stages were best (5.67-6.78 of 10).
agent_test: Equal tokens: store past cases with and without an explicit relation-name field; query with and without the relation name; score share of relational vs same-domain retrievals.

claim: Domain labels (e.g. 'anatomy') do not help relational or domain retrieval, so the effect is specific to relational labels, not any label (Bayes factors 0.30-0.39 vs intercept-only).
agent_test: Control arm: add a same-length domain tag instead of a relation name; expect no gain.

claim: In Jamrozik and Gentner (2020), test labels helped only when placed before the test passage (labels after the passage did not, p=.188), while at encoding the position (before or after) made no clear difference. In a separate perceptual search task (Lupyan and Spivey 2010), a spoken label's benefit disappeared when it preceded the display by more than about 1600 ms.
agent_test: Place the relation name before vs after the case in the prompt at equal tokens.
audit_note: In Jamrozik and Gentner, label position mattered only for labels at test (after the passage n.s., p=.188); at encoding before vs after did not differ (3.19 vs 3.40 relational matches), and the 1600 ms decay comes from a perceptual 'five' search task (Lupyan and Spivey), not relational labelling.
claim_before_audit: Relational labels help best when placed before the item they apply to; test labels placed after the passage did not help (p=.188). Label effects are also transient in time (gone beyond about 1600 ms).

claim: Giving two cases a shared contrastive label ('brace') raised transfer in 5-7 year olds (OR 3.15, N=64) and persisted 2-5 days (near transfer OR 2.57, far construction OR 1.60, N=116); the label did not help the immediate repair task.
agent_test: Compare-then-name: show two aligned cases, then name the contrast; compare with compare-only at equal tokens.

claim: Comparison of highly alignable cases helps learning independently of labels, and label effects add to it (no alignment x label interaction); label gains held on far transfer where alignment did not.
agent_test: 2x2 on the agent: aligned vs unaligned example pairs x relation name vs none.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Relational language helps preschoolers map relations (top/middle/bottom; 'red is on the left' 57% -> 79%) and the advantage persists about 2 days. Figures are second-hand via the 2025 introduction.
agent_test: Check LLM sensitivity to spatial relation words on mapping tasks.

claim: Relational labels did not help 12-month-olds: no benefit for 'same/different' (N=64) or object labels (N=48); label and salience are confounded. Gerson & Woodward 2014 (not opened) reports label help for action goals.
agent_test: Not directly testable; warns that labels help only when the learner already has a usable relation vocabulary.

claim: Easy-to-name category features speed rule-based category learning; strong in adults (95.8% vs 87.3%, d=1.06), weak and non-significant in children overall (71.0 vs 65.9, p=.118).
agent_test: Rename features with short consistent names vs opaque names in rule-induction tasks.

claim: Redundant nonsense labels speed novel category learning (Lupyan, Rakison & McClelland 2007) but an online replication in adults failed.
agent_test: Do not assume labels help for easily distinguished categories; test per task.

claim: Redundant labels during matching make later sorting more categorical and more aligned between people (alignment .20 vs .11/.12, Exp 1); Exp 2 (N=122) replicated alignment but categoricality was weaker and ns vs no-labels. Re-read (d09): Exp 1 N=129, Exp 2 N=122; categoricality fully mediates alignment in Exp 1 only; diversity effect mixed.
agent_test: Shared label vocabulary across agent samples: measure agreement between runs.

claim: Label effects on perception of unseen objects are contested: Lupyan & Ward 2013 reported a boost, a 2026 preregistered EEG study (N=20) found none.
agent_test: Low priority; perception is out of scope for a text agent.

claim: Label-feedback hypothesis: an active word feeds back to modulate processing online; the effect is transient, so label proximity to the use site matters.
agent_test: Keep relation names adjacent to use sites; test repeating the name near the question.

claim: Relation words are context-mutable (verbs shift more than nouns) and content pulls operations off course (addition 82% for symmetric vs 61% for asymmetric pairs). Both figures second-hand.
agent_test: Include a one-line definition of each relation name; check on content-conflicting items.

claim: Without any relation labels GPT-3 matched or beat UCLA students on digit matrices (OR 1.88), letter strings (OR 1.76) and verbal analogies; story analogies were above chance for near (p=.0039) but not far (p=.065) pairs.
agent_test: Baseline for which tasks need naming at all.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: That zero-shot analogy competence is brittle: permuted or symbol alphabets drop GPT-3/3.5/4 while humans stay flat; moving the blank collapses GPT-4 digit matrices (0.81 -> 0.48) while humans do not (0.715 -> 0.771).
agent_test: Perturb the surface form of each test and track accuracy at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Explicitly naming entity attributes lets a text-only LM solve visual matrix analogies: GPT-3 175B 77.2% with ordinal naming vs 28.2% ASCII quasi-image and 51.8% random-word naming; decomposition adds more (OPT-125M 22.2 -> 45.6%).
agent_test: Closest LLM test of naming: vary naming quality (ordinal vs random vs none) on a relational task at equal tokens.

claim: Self-generated analogous problems before solving beat fixed-example CoT modestly (GSM8K GPT-3.5: 5-shot CoT 75.0 vs 75.8-77.8%; MATH 33.0 vs 33.9-37.3%); larger gains for weaker models. This is self-recall, not relation naming.
agent_test: Add a recall-then-solve arm vs fixed examples at equal tokens.

claim: Thought Propagation (solve analogous problems and reuse their solutions) reports +12% shortest-path, +15% agent planning; abstract only.
agent_test: Replicate from the full paper before use.

claim: LLMs fail far analogies with surface distractors: ARN GPT-4 far/near 29.1% vs human 91.4%, far/far 57.1%; models lean on association (Stevenson 2023, age level drops 1-2 years when controlled). Also AnaloBench: GPT-4 89.1/66.5/60.7 vs human 96.0/72.5/73.3 at 1/10/30 sentences; retrieval near random. Relation-vector injection raised far analogies most (d03).
agent_test: Test far-analogy items with surface distractors; check whether a relation name in the prompt closes the gap.
audit_note: ARN, AnaloBench, Stevenson and the function-vector paper match; 'most' for far analogies is a mild reading of the function-vector results (near analogies were flat or slightly lower), and the function-vector paper is a small-model (GPT-J, LLaMA) study.

claim: Humans beat GPT-4 on ConceptARC relational concepts: Above/Below .90 vs .23, Same/Different .93 vs .20, Count .86 vs .03. 2025 update (d08): o3 text accuracy 77.1% vs human 73%, but about 27% of correct-output rules are unintended or incorrect (humans about 7%); the 2023 gap is mostly closed in accuracy, not in rule quality.
agent_test: Evaluate a naming scaffold on ConceptARC groups.

claim: Mechanistic: relation information sits in mid-upper layers; failures are missing relation information or failure to apply it to new entities; patching fixes up to 38.4% of failures. Re-opened (d01): the 38.4% is Gemma-7B (Qwen2.5-14B +35.6%); the paper gives no split of failures into missing vs not applied and tests no prompt fix.
agent_test: Suggests stating the relation explicitly supplies missing information; test via a naming arm.

claim: No study found tests Gentner's relational-label effect or Lupyan's label feedback directly on LLMs; Hu et al. 2023 is the closest. Gap search (constrained, APIs rate-limited) found none either; nearest prompt-level tests are KnowledgePrompts TKP (d02) and StoryAnalogy template C (d06).
agent_test: A direct test is the main open item.

claim: Stating the shared relation in the prompt (targeted-knowledge prompt) raised accuracy for 6 of 9 models on 15K analogies; GPT-3.5-Turbo 45.70 -> 55.25, FlanT5 36.47 -> 44.26; Zephyr fell 29.46 -> 15.83. Extra relevant text without the relation did not help (GPT-3.5 38.3-38.8).
agent_test: Relation statement vs equal-length neutral text vs none, across at least three model sizes; expect model-dependent sign.

claim: A prompt that tells the model to weigh relations over shared entities raised story-analogy identification for FlanT5-xxl (41.2 -> 48.0) and GPT-3.5 (33.7 -> 44.0) but little for LLaMa and ChatGPT.
agent_test: Add a one-line relation-over-surface instruction to the analogy retrieval step; compare with plain wording.

claim: Naming and structuring objects helps beyond RAVEN: GPT-4 ARC 13/50 -> 23/50 with object JSON, 81 -> 97 of 400 on the full set, and reasoning was correct in 20 of 23 object solves vs 3 of 13 grid solves. Adding edge (relation) information lowered scores (23 -> 16 with CoT).
agent_test: Name entities first; add relation edges only for the few relations that matter and check for overload.

claim: 2025 reasoning models reach human-level ConceptARC text accuracy (o3 77.1%, humans 73%) but about 27% of correct outputs rest on unintended or incorrect rules vs about 7% for humans; accuracy alone overstates competence in text and understates it in vision.
agent_test: Grade the stated relation, not only the answer, when testing any naming scaffold.

claim: Injecting a relation representation (fine-tuned function vector) lifts far analogies most (GPT-J far 42.5 -> 61.0; LLaMa-3.1 57.5 -> 74.0) with small losses on near ones (LLaMa-3.1 87.5 -> 85.0); label-prompt steering alone was weak (18% vs 75%). Activation-level, not prompt-level.
agent_test: Not reachable by prompt; use only as a direction for what a relation name should encode.

claim: Lupyan's 2026 stance (Perspectives on Psychological Science) is that language supplies compact, culturally evolved abstractions to any learner including AI; Liu & Lupyan's 2026 review says whether language drives or merely reflects cross-domain mappings is unresolved. Positions, not measurements.
agent_test: None; background.

claim: Gap search could not find a direct LLM test of relation name vs domain tag vs none, of name placement, or of compare-then-name; nor any extra replication of Jamrozik 2020 or Lupyan 2007 beyond the failed online replication. Search was limited by rate limits, so this is unproven absence.
agent_test: Run the direct test (see K01, K02, K03).
